claims.claim: 50,000 concurrent WebSockets is a moderate load for Node, and matching within 2 seconds depends on how you design the matcher, not on the language
claims.why: The benchmarks top out at 256 HTTP connections and include no WebSocket or matchmaking test, so capacity at 50,000 connections can't be checked.

claims.claim: A single Node process can hold far more than 5–10k connections when connections are mostly idle
claims.why: No test measures how many idle long-lived connections a server can hold; the most connections tested was 256.

claims.claim: Socket.IO adds protocol overhead compared with plain ws
claims.why: Neither Socket.IO nor ws was benchmarked.

claims.claim: Elixir's runtime is excellent at holding many connections, and its advantages matter at millions of connections, not 50,000
claims.measured: I/O wait at 256 connections: elixir-phoenix 18,711 req/s, 160 MB peak
claims.why: The only many-connection test is 256 connections, nowhere near the tens of thousands to millions the claim is about, and it doesn't measure connection-holding capacity.

claims.claim: Go would use less memory per connection than Node
claims.measured: I/O wait at 256 connections, peak memory: go-gin 16 MB, go-nethttp 15 MB vs node-express 68 MB, node-fastify 69 MB; idle: Go 2 MB vs Node 38–43 MB
claims.why: With 256 concurrent connections Go's peak memory was about a quarter of Node's, which points the way the claim says.

claims.claim: Go handles CPU-heavy work better than Node
claims.measured: fib(20): go-gin 18,218 and go-nethttp 15,093 req/s vs node-express 7,213 and node-fastify 8,308 req/s
claims.why: On the CPU-bound test Go did about 2–2.5 times the throughput of the Node frameworks.

claims.claim: At 50,000 connections Go's memory saving doesn't matter
claims.why: Memory at 50,000 connections wasn't measured, so it can't be checked whether the gap stays small in absolute terms.

claims.claim: Large synchronous JSON handling or matching work inside a gateway blocks Node's event loop and delays every player on that pod
claims.why: The benchmarks don't test mixed workloads, so there is no measure of how blocking work affects other connections' latency.

claims.claim: Load tests showing Node can't keep event-loop lag down at 100,000 connections are unlikely for this workload
claims.why: Event-loop lag and behaviour at 100,000 connections weren't measured.
